cards.back: A sample where every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected. It is the best way to avoid bias.
A sample where members volunteer to participate. Often biased because those with strong opinions are more likely to respond.
A sample chosen by a rule, such as selecting every 10th person on a list. Can be easy to implement but may introduce bias if a pattern exists.
The population is divided into groups (strata) that share a characteristic, and a random sample is taken from each group. Ensures all subgroups are represented.
The population is divided into clusters, and entire clusters are randomly selected. All members of chosen clusters are included in the sample.
A sample that selects members of the population who are easy to reach. Usually biased because it does not represent the whole population.
An error that causes a sample to overrepresent or underrepresent part of the population. Biased samples lead to invalid conclusions.

cards.front: How can you create an unbiased random sample?
cards.back: Assign a unique number to each member of the population, then use a random number generator to select the sample. Every member has an equal chance.
It only includes people who are easily accessible, leaving out those who are harder to reach. This can produce results that do not reflect the entire population.
cards.front: Why is a convenience sample often biased?

cards.back: A method where a treatment is imposed on individuals to measure its effect. Experiments can establish cause-and-effect relationships.
cards.front: What is an [[kw:experiment]] in data collection?

cards.back: A method where individuals are observed and variables are measured without controlling the environment. It can show associations but not causation.
An investigation where every member of a sample is asked one or more questions. Surveys rely on self‑reported data.
A method that uses a model to reproduce the conditions of a real‑world process. Useful when actual experiments are impractical or dangerous.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:biased question]] in a survey?
cards.back: A question worded in a way that encourages a particular response or makes it hard to answer truthfully. It can lead to inaccurate survey results.
Split it into two separate questions that each address only one issue. This allows respondents to give accurate answers to each part.
cards.front: How can you fix a double‑barreled survey question?

cards.back: A study in which two groups are compared under identical conditions except for one variable (the treatment). One group receives the treatment; the other (control group) does not.
The group in an experiment that receives no treatment or a placebo. It serves as a baseline for comparison to see if the treatment had an effect.
The group in an experiment that receives the treatment being tested.
Randomly assigning subjects to the treatment group or control group. This minimizes bias and makes the groups similar in all ways before the treatment is applied.
cards.front: What does [[kw:randomization]] mean in an experiment?

cards.back: A controlled experiment where subjects are randomly assigned to the control group or the treatment group. This design can establish cause-and-effect relationships.
A harmless, fake treatment (like a sugar pill) that looks like the real treatment. It is given to the control group to prevent psychological effects from influencing results.

In an experiment, a treatment is imposed and subjects are randomly assigned to groups (can show causation). In an observational study, subjects are observed without imposing a treatment (can only show correlation).
cards.front: How does an experiment differ from an observational study?
Why can observational studies not prove causation?
cards.back: Because the groups may differ in ways other than the variable being studied. [[imp:Confounding variables]] can affect the results, so we can only say there is an association, not that one variable causes the other.
A variable other than the treatment that could affect the results of an experiment. It makes it hard to determine the true cause of an effect.
Repeating an experiment under the same or similar conditions. It confirms that results are not just a one-time fluke and increases reliability.

cards.front: Why is a large [[kw:sample size]] important in an experiment?
cards.back: Larger samples reduce the effect of chance and make the results more reliable. Small samples can be skewed by a few unusual individuals.

An experimental design where subjects are first grouped by a similar characteristic (like age or gender), and then within each block, randomly assigned to treatment or control. This controls for the effect of that characteristic.

Not a randomized comparative experiment — patients chose their own group. This is an observational study with self-selection. The conclusion may not be valid because healthier patients might have chosen to take the supplement.
cards.front: Identify the flaw: 'Patients chose whether to take vitamin C; after a year, the vitamin C group had 15% lower cholesterol.'

cards.back: Gender is completely confounded with the treatment. We don't know if the difference is due to the gum or to gender. The design should randomly assign gum/placebo within each gender group.
cards.front: Identify the flaw: '10,000 overweight people: females get the new weight‑loss gum, males get a placebo. Females lose more weight.'

cards.back: A phenomenon where people experience a real improvement simply because they believe they are receiving a treatment, even if it's a placebo. A control group with a placebo accounts for this effect.
